In hiring, I often use a CS degree form a decent school as a proxy for IQ, because in some CS programs you have to pass an algorithms class which is simply not possible for low IQ people unless they weasel their way through somehow. A better degree program just won't allow that to happen. That said, though, I have met a lot of CS majors who fit your description. The worst example is kids who went to undergrad programs at top-ten schools and were not smart enough to do well without killing themselves studying. This is in contrast to other CS majors like many friends of mine who went to a mid-tier college, but learned programming or sysadmin skills prior to college as a hobby, worked legitimate internships and coops during college, and did not waste time trying to earn superficial accolades in favor of actually honing their craft independently during college. That to me is the best CS candidate-- one who has a degree but where the classwork only formed maybe 30% of their professional development. The rest should come from internships, projects or independent study/research, and self-guided learning based on a pre-established passion for the field (hobby). It's OK if a candidate does not have a CS degree, but if they also do not have a STEM degree of any kind, it is going to make the interview process much more difficult for them because we have to make sure they are not bluffing on all kinds of fundamental stuff that is pretty important when it comes to functioning on the job. A self-taught programmer after 1 year will potentially make all kinds of retarded design decisions on the job that someone who is at least aware of CS theory will probably not.
